title: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos chosen to succeed Lagarde at the ECB
excerpt: Euro area leaders have backed former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernández de Cos to replace Christine Lagarde as head of the European Central Bank.
content_html:
European leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday agreed that Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain, will be the next president of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde when she steps down in February.

The agreement was confirmed by an EU diplomat and by French President Emmanuel Macron, the Associated Press reported. The European Parliament and the ECB's governing council still have to review the choice, steps AP described as formalities, and the ABC reported final sign-off is expected at a summit in December.

Who he is

Hernández de Cos, 55, is the general manager of the Bank for International Settlements in Basel. He previously worked as an ECB staff member and as the Bank of Spain's chief economist before leading that bank, a role that gave him a seat on the ECB's rate-setting council from 2018 to 2024.

His main rival for the post was Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank, who is regarded as more hawkish on inflation.

Lagarde's early exit

Lagarde announced on 30 October that she would leave on 7 February, about nine months before her eight-year term was due to end. She said she wanted to speak more freely on matters beyond monetary policy.

According to the ABC, her successor's first interest rate meeting will be on 18 March.

Leaders also settled two other senior ECB jobs. Princeton economist Markus Brunnermeier is set to replace chief economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May, and French economist Laurence Boone will take the board seat being vacated by Germany's Isabel Schnabel in January, AP reported.

Policy outlook

The appointment comes as euro area inflation runs at about 4 per cent, double the bank's 2 per cent target. The ECB meets again on 17 December under Lagarde, and AP reported a rate rise remains possible.

Analysts at Commerzbank who reviewed his speeches placed Hernández de Cos among the bank's doves, meaning he tends to favour lower interest rates. Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner told AP that "many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president".

Other economists expect little sudden change in direction. Before the decision, economists at broker Mizuho described him to Reuters as "a consensus-builder rather than an obvious policy driver".

For Australian readers, the ECB's decisions shape borrowing costs and currency moves in one of the world's largest economies, which flow through to global markets and the Australian dollar.
